BOOK ENTRY
A complete seven crowned by rest — the week itself, and the unit at every scale the law counts: the land's seventh year, the seven sevens to Jubilee. Hebrew counts "seven sabbaths" (shabbatot) where Deuteronomy counts the same span as "seven weeks" (shavuot); Greek calls the week the sabbath — "twice in the sabbath" (dis tou sabbatou) is twice a week, and every "first day of the week" is "one of the sabbaths" (mia sabbatōn). The rest is the completing member of the whole unit.

SCRIPTURE REFERENCES PRINTED WITH THE ENTRY
(Lev 23:15 with Deut 16:9; Lev 25:2-8; Luke 18:12; Matt 28:1; Heb 4:9) · see The Sabbath, ch. 32

AVAILABLE KJV EXCERPTS
Leviticus 23:15 — And ye shall count unto you from the morrow after the sabbath, from the day that ye brought the sheaf of the wave offering; seven sabbaths shall be complete:
Leviticus 25:2 — Speak unto the children of Israel, and say unto them, When ye come into the land which I give you, then shall the land keep a sabbath unto the LORD.
Leviticus 25:3 — Six years thou shalt sow thy field, and six years thou shalt prune thy vineyard, and gather in the fruit thereof;
Leviticus 25:4 — But in the seventh year shall be a sabbath of rest unto the land, a sabbath for the LORD: thou shalt neither sow thy field, nor prune thy vineyard.
Leviticus 25:5 — That which groweth of its own accord of thy harvest thou shalt not reap, neither gather the grapes of thy vine undressed: for it is a year of rest unto the land.
Leviticus 25:6 — And the sabbath of the land shall be meat for you; for thee, and for thy servant, and for thy maid, and for thy hired servant, and for thy stranger that sojourneth with thee,
Leviticus 25:7 — And for thy cattle, and for the beast that are in thy land, shall all the increase thereof be meat.
Leviticus 25:8 — And thou shalt number seven sabbaths of years unto thee, seven times seven years; and the space of the seven sabbaths of years shall be unto thee forty and nine years.
Luke 18:12 — I fast twice in the week, I give tithes of all that I possess.
Matthew 28:1 — In the end of the sabbath, as it began to dawn toward the first day of the week, came Mary Magdalene and the other Mary to see the sepulchre.
Hebrews 4:9 — There remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God.

SOURCE EXCERPTS FROM THE BOOK EXPLAINING AND DEMONSTRATING ITS METHOD
SOURCE EXCERPT: books/symbolic-language/01-introduction.adoc — opening

Shortly after feeding the five thousand, Jesus gave a hard teaching in the synagogue at Capernaum (John 6:59): “Except ye eat the flesh of the Son of man, and drink his blood, ye have no life in you… He that eateth my flesh, and drinketh my blood, dwelleth in me, and I in him” (John 6:53, 56).
After He said this, many of His disciples murmured — “This is an hard saying; who can hear it?” — and “from that time many of his disciples went back, and walked no more with him” (John 6:60, 66).
It was so bad that Jesus turned to the twelve and asked whether they would also go away.

It was a hard saying because those who heard it did not know the symbolic language of the Scriptures, and took it over-literally, saying: “How can this man give us his flesh to eat?” (John 6:52).
Which prompts the question: why would Jesus speak in a manner that drives people away?
Why not speak plainly?

He did it to fulfill the Scriptures, which prophesied that He would speak in parables.
When he spoke publicly he always used parables — “without a parable spake he not unto them” (Matthew 13:34) — and only with his closest disciples did he explain their meaning.
Even so, when he gave the parables of the kingdom his own disciples did not understand, and Jesus rebuked them for it. The rebuke was fair because the keys were already in the Old Testament: the “dark sayings of old” that the psalm said he would utter (Mark 4:13; Psalm 78:2-3; Matthew 13:35). That exam waits a chapter ahead: The Parables of the Kingdom. [Footnote: The Parables of the Kingdom chapter derives each parable of Matthew 13 from the Old Testament alone.]

In other words, Scripture prophesied that the message would be encrypted in parables and decoded with the Old Testament.
If you think you can read the New Testament without an intimate understanding of the Old, chances are you will walk away like the masses — either by interpreting it in a way you reject, or by misinterpreting it in a way you can accept, and facing the same consequences either way.

The first hearers of the apostles knew better.
When Paul preached in Berea, Luke recorded how the hearers received him — and graded them for it:

These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.

They tested Paul against the Old Testament, and Scripture calls that nobility.
How many today search the Old Testament to see whether their understanding of Paul is true?
The order has quietly reversed: Paul, as we understand him, has become the judge of the very Scriptures he was judged by.
And the test is not for Paul only — your understanding of any verse must be tested against every other verse, for “at the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall the matter be established” (Deuteronomy 19:15): one verse cannot make a doctrine.

The Bible provides two symbolic words, meat and milk, to describe its teachings, and if you do not do the work to churn the milk into meat, you will remain immature at best — and at worst turn away entirely, like the crowds in Jesus’ day.

The purpose of this book is to teach you how I learned to chew the word of God and test everything.
It is a repeatable, reproducible process that has yielded more pearls of wisdom — and more appreciation for the supernatural structure of the word of God — than I could possibly fit in one book.
We will go through the process systematically and apply it to dozens of symbolic words, starting with meat and milk.
But first we must prepare the ground by explaining the difference between a word and a symbol.

===== NEXT SOURCE EXCERPT =====

SOURCE EXCERPT: books/symbolic-language/02-the-parables-of-the-kingdom.adoc — opening through How the Exam Is Taken

At the end of the seven parables of the kingdom, Jesus gave His hearers an exam of one question, and they passed it: “Yea, Lord.”
It had not started that way.
At the first parable — the key to all of them — His own disciples stumbled, and He rebuked them: “Know ye not this parable? and how then will ye know all parables?” (Mark 4:13).

Stop and weigh that rebuke.
A teacher may not be astonished that students fail an exam on material they were never given; His astonishment is only just if the answers were already on the table.
They were, and He said where.

The psalm He fulfills by teaching in parables locates the material in the past, not the future: “I will open my mouth in a parable: I will utter dark sayings of old: which we have heard and known, and our fathers have told us” (Psalm 78:2-3; Matthew 13:35).
And the Scriptures the disciples grew up on do not merely contain parables — they decode them in front of the reader and expect him to grade himself.

Nathan told David a story about a ewe lamb; David judged its villain to death without seeing his own face — “the man that hath done this thing shall surely die” (2 Samuel 12:5) — and Nathan handed him the key in four words: “Thou art the man” (2 Samuel 12:7).
Isaiah sang a parable of a vineyard, then handed over the key: “the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel” (Isaiah 5:7).
Ezekiel told a riddle of two eagles and a vine, and God's next word is the very question Jesus would ask on the boat: “Know ye not what these things mean?” — followed by the answer, “the king of Babylon is come to Jerusalem” (Ezekiel 17:2, 12).

The exam is closed-book in one direction only: everything needed sits in the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms.
Take each parable, then, the way a disciple on the shore had to take it — derive the meaning from the Scriptures he already had, write it down, and only then let the Teacher grade the work.
That is how this chapter will read them, and it will keep score.
More broadly, it will establish the principle of how to decode all Scripture using the full body of the word.

Before the first parable, fix the procedure, because it is this book's whole method in miniature.
Take the parable's own words — sower, seed, ground, thorns, fowls — and search the Scriptures for the same words and phrases, everywhere they fall.
Where Scripture has already defined a term out loud — Isaiah's own key, above: the vineyard is the house of Israel — that definition is not local color for one passage; it holds, and it holds uniformly, or parables could not be decoded at all.

Next, weigh what you gathered before you lean on it.
One verse makes a candidate, not a key: a symbol is established when the pattern spans Moses and the prophets and the psalms — independent witnesses carrying the same figure, with no counter-text standing against them.
That standard is what makes the rebuke in the boat just, and it measures its weight: Jesus did not upbraid the twelve for missing an obscurity; seed and ground and thorns and fowls were established patterns, laid down across the whole of the Scriptures read to them every sabbath since childhood.
The better attested the pattern, the more accountable the hearer.

The difference between their seat and yours matters.
The disciple on the shore had his memory and the weekly reading; you have the whole text searchable in moments — a concordance, a search bar, and tools that can gather every use of a word while you frame your next question.
Recall was never the point of the exam, and now it is not even the obstacle: the test is not whether you remember the matches, but whether you go look for them.

===== NEXT SOURCE EXCERPT =====

SOURCE EXCERPT: books/symbolic-language/02-the-parables-of-the-kingdom.adoc — The Sower, Derived and Graded

“Behold, a sower went forth to sow” (Matthew 13:3).
Close the Gospels; what could a hearer of Moses and the prophets make of that?
Start with the seed, which Isaiah had defined in one breath with the rain:

For as the rain cometh down… that it may give seed to the sower, and bread to the eater: so shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth…

The word is the seed to the sower and the bread to the eater — one verse, both figures.
And Moses had sung the same rain long before: “My doctrine shall drop as the rain, my speech shall distil as the dew” (Deuteronomy 32:2) — what falls from heaven to make the ground bear is teaching.

Next the ground.
Jeremiah had already preached this parable as a command: “Break up your fallow ground, and sow not among thorns” — and his very next sentence names the soil: “take away the foreskins of your heart” (Jeremiah 4:3-4) — plowing and circumcising, one operation in two figures: remove the blocking flesh so the seed can enter.
Hosea gives the same order in the same words: “break up your fallow ground: for it is time to seek the LORD” (Hosea 10:12).
The ground is the heart, and the thorns were choking Judah's heart seven centuries before the sermon by the sea — and the thorns have a pedigree older still, for they are the curse-ground's own crop: “thorns also and thistles shall it (the ground) bring forth to thee” (Genesis 3:18), what the cursed earth grows where food should stand.

Now derive what the thorns mean, for the Old Testament assigns that too.
Read the sentence they grow in: the same curse that gives the ground its thorns sentences the man to anxious toil for his bread — “in sorrow shalt thou eat of it… in the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread” (Genesis 3:17, 19) — the thorns spring up in the field of the struggle for a living.
And that pair of weeds — thorn and thistle together — returns exactly once more in the Hebrew Scriptures, and Hosea builds the whole indictment around it:

Israel is an empty vine, he bringeth forth fruit unto himself: according to the multitude of his fruit he hath increased the altars; according to the goodness of his land they have made goodly images.
Their heart is divided; now shall they be found faulty…

The high places also of Aven, the sin of Israel, shall be destroyed: the thorn and the thistle shall come up on their altars; and they shall say to the mountains, Cover us; and to the hills, Fall on us.

Increase, a divided heart, and the curse-ground's own crop sprouting on the altars: riches choking the heart is Hosea's picture before it is the parable's.

Isaiah's vineyard tells the same story, and he graded it himself.
The vineyard planted with the choicest vine gave wild grapes instead, and the sentence fell:

And I will lay it waste: it shall not be pruned, nor digged; but there shall come up briers and thorns: I will also command the clouds that they rain no rain upon it.

Isaiah then hands over the key:

For the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel, and the men of Judah his pleasant plant: and he looked for judgment, but behold oppression; for righteousness, but behold a cry.

The vineyard is Israel, and its briers and thorns are men — the woes that follow name them, person by person:

Woe unto them that join house to house, that lay field to field, till there be no place, that they may be placed alone in the midst of the earth!

Here is the monopoly-builder — buying house after house and field after field until no one else has a place, alone in the middle of everything he has swallowed.

Woe unto them that rise up early in the morning, that they may follow strong drink; that continue until night, till wine inflame them!
And the harp, and the viol, the tabret, and pipe, and wine, are in their feasts: but they regard not the work of the LORD, neither consider the operation of his hands.

Here is the pleasure-lover — feasting from morning drink to evening music, past all notice of God.
Riches and pleasures came up where fruit should have stood: Isaiah graded the thorns seven centuries before the sermon by the sea.

Even the stony ground was on record, for the heart God promises to replace is “the stony heart” (Ezekiel 36:26).
And why is the exchange a heart of flesh for a heart of stone?
Because flesh is ground: adam was formed “of the dust of the ground,” adamah (Genesis 2:7) — the man is named for the soil he is — and he was sent forth “to till the ground from whence he was taken” (Genesis 3:23), so the Sower's field was staked out in Eden.
No one plows rock — “will one plow there with oxen?” (Amos 6:12) — and the very oracle that promises the heart of flesh promises its plowing: “I am for you… and ye shall be tilled and sown” (Ezekiel 36:9).
The seed that found “no deepness of earth” on stone takes root in flesh: the law once carved on “tables of stone” written now “in fleshy tables of the heart” (2 Corinthians 3:3) — “ye are God's husbandry” (1 Corinthians 3:9).

What does ground bring forth when the seed takes?
Grass — “all flesh is grass” (Isaiah 40:6) — a symbol with a chapter of its own.

What of the fowls that devour the wayside seed?
The first time birds descend on a covenant in Scripture, they come as devourers: “when the fowls came down upon the carcases, Abram drove them away” (Genesis 15:11) — uninvited, snatching at the covenant sacrifice, driven off by the covenant man.
In Egypt, Joseph heard a dream of birds eating baked bread out of a basket and graded it without hesitation as a sentence of death (Genesis 40:17-19).
Birds that snatch what was given out of its place are the enemy's agents; a boy raised on Genesis could have written that down.

.The Teacher grades the derivation

|===
| Element | Derived from the Law and the Prophets | The Teacher's key

| Seed
| The word — rain-borne seed, rain-borne doctrine (Isa 55:10-11; Deut 32:2)
| “The seed is the word of God” (Luke 8:11)

| Ground
| The heart — plowed, circumcised, tilled and sown (Jer 4:3-4; Hos 10:12; Ezek 36:9, 26; Gen 2:7)
| The word “sown in his heart” (Matt 13:19)

| Fowls
| The devourers on the covenant and on the bread (Gen 15:11; 40:17-19)
| “Then cometh the wicked one, and catcheth away that which was sown” (Matt 13:19)

| Thorns
| The curse-crop; riches dividing the heart (Gen 3:17-19; Hos 10:1-8; Isa 5:6-12)
| “The care of this world, and the deceitfulness of riches, choke the word” (Matt 13:22)
|===

Four for four — Isaiah's answer, Jeremiah's, Abram's, Hosea's — and not one of the four needed a word Jesus had not yet spoken.
His astonishment in Mark 4:13 was just.

Yet let me be fair, for I would have fared no better.
Handed the parable with no Bible in reach, I would have failed it as completely as any man on the shore.
With a Bible and a printed concordance — and the assurance that the answer was in there somewhere — the derivation above might have cost me days, or months.
It is only with modern tools that I can derive the interpretation independently at all, without leaning on any man's commentary.

Daniel was told to seal the words “even to the time of the end,” when “many shall run to and fro, and knowledge shall be increased” (Daniel 12:4).
The running to and fro is through the Scriptures themselves — and the knowledge increased is this.

PRIOR FINDINGS ACCEPTED BY THIS PROVIDER AND MODEL IN FROZEN RUNS
No prior findings were supplied.

SOURCE: books/symbolic-language/32-the-sabbath.adoc

Ask what the word sabbath names and every answer points at one day in seven.
But the law counts sabbaths — and watch what it says about them:

And ye shall count unto you from the morrow after the sabbath, from the day that ye brought the sheaf of the wave offering; seven sabbaths shall be complete.

A sabbath can be complete — the word is temimot, whole, unblemished, the word the law uses for a sacrifice without defect — and whatever can be complete can be incomplete.
A day cannot be partially itself; it is or it is not.
Only a span can be whole or broken.
The thing Israel counts toward Pentecost is not seven rest-days; it is seven unbroken sevens — and the word for that unit is sabbath.

This is not an inference; the law says it twice, once in each vocabulary.
The same omer count that Leviticus gives as “seven sabbaths” stands in Deuteronomy as:

Seven weeks shalt thou number unto thee: begin to number the seven weeks from such time as thou beginnest to put the sickle to the corn.

One command, one festival, one count — sabbath in Leviticus, week in Deuteronomy.
The equation is stated by parallel statute: a sabbath is a week — the complete seven, of which the day of rest is the seventh part.

Hebrew is not short of week-words.
When Laban says “fulfil her week” (Genesis 29:27), the word is shavua — a bare seven of days — and it is Deuteronomy's word for the omer count itself.
Leviticus had that word available and wrote shabbatot instead.
The choice is part of the statute: a shavua is any seven; a sabbath is the seven structured by rest — six days of labor closed by a holy seventh — and only a structured seven can be temimot, whole or broken.

The objection is natural: perhaps sabbath is simply the rest-day's name, borrowed loosely for the span it closes.
Scripture answers with the calendar's own grammar, because naming a block of days by its marked day is exactly how the feasts talk:

In the first month, in the fourteenth day of the month, ye shall have the passover, a feast of seven days; unleavened bread shall be eaten.

The passover is one day's sacrifice, slain on the fourteenth — yet Ezekiel names the whole seven by it, and the letters under “seven days” are shavuot yamim: a week of days.
Luke records the same usage in Greek: “the feast of unleavened bread drew nigh, which is called the Passover” (Luke 22:1).
One marked day lends its name to its seven.
The passover names the week it opens; the sabbath names the week it crowns.

If sabbath named only a day, it could not stretch; a unit stretches.
The law runs the same word at year-scale without changing gear: the seventh year is “a sabbath of rest unto the land” (Leviticus 25:4), and the jubilee is reached by counting the unit squared:

And thou shalt number seven sabbaths of years unto thee, seven times seven years; and the space of the seven sabbaths of years shall be unto thee forty and nine years.

Sabbaths of years — the word takes whatever tick the count assigns it: a seven of days, a seven of years, a seven of sevens.

The days of Scripture have no names.
Creation numbers them — first, second, third — and the numbering never stops: in the whole Bible no day of the week bears a name except the seventh.
The numbers live inside the sabbath, and the temple's own hymnal shows it.
The Septuagint carries the psalms Israel sang through the week, and the titles count every day as a position in the sabbath-unit: Psalm 24 is sung “on the first day of the week” — tēs mias sabbatōn, day one of the sabbaths — Psalm 48 “on the second” (deutera sabbatou), Psalm 94 “for the fourth” (tetradi sabbatōn), and Psalm 93 “for the day before the sabbath” — the prosabbaton, the fore-sabbath.
Mark dates the crucifixion evening by that same liturgical word: “it was the preparation, that is, the day before the sabbath” (Mark 15:42).
Centuries before the Gospels were written, Israel was numbering its days as members of the sabbath.

The Gospels inherit the idiom whole, and translation has hidden it.
The Pharisee in the parable boasts, “I fast twice in the week” (Luke 18:12) — but what he says is dis tou sabbatou: twice in the sabbath.
No man fasts twice in a day; he fasts twice in the seven — and he calls the seven the sabbath.
Every “first day of the week” in the resurrection accounts is literally “one of the sabbaths” — mia sabbatōn (Matthew 28:1; Mark 16:2; Luke 24:1; John 20:1; Acts 20:7; 1 Corinthians 16:2) — the week's first day named as a day of the sabbath-unit. [Footnote: The Hebrew Matthew reads “on the first day of the week” with shavua, the week-word — the old translator rendered the Greek's “one of the sabbaths” by its meaning: the unit of seven.]
Matthew holds both senses of the word in a single verse:

In the end of the sabbath [the day], as it began to dawn toward the first day of the week [literally, “one of the sabbaths” — the unit], came Mary Magdalene and the other Mary to see the sepulchre.

The language itself testifies: sabbath names the seven, and the seventh day is its crown.

If one word names both the week and its day, the text needs a way to say which — and it has one, the same one it uses for the month.
Chodesh does the same double duty: the month, and the renewed-moon day that heads it.
Ezekiel disambiguates both words in one verse, with one construction:

The gate of the inner court that looketh toward the east shall be shut the six working days; but on the sabbath it shall be opened, and in the day of the new moon it shall be opened.

The Hebrew of the two clauses is identical: b'yom ha-shabbat… b'yom ha-chodesh — on the day of the sabbath, on the day of the new moon.
Each unit owns a marked day, and the text names that day by the genitive.
This is the grammar of the fourth commandment itself: “Remember the sabbath day” (Exodus 20:8) is yom ha-shabbat — the day of the sabbath — a redundancy if sabbath named only a day, and exact if the sabbath is the unit that has one.
Luke writes the rest day the same way in Greek — tē hēmera tōn sabbatōn, the day of the sabbaths (Luke 4:16; Acts 13:14; 16:13) — while the other days are numbered into the unit: the first of the sabbath, the second, the fourth.

When the law wants the resting member itself, it has a second marker: it doubles the word.
“The seventh day is the sabbath of rest” — shabbat shabbaton (Exodus 31:15; 35:2; Leviticus 23:3); the Day of Atonement receives the doubled name (Leviticus 16:31), and so does the land's seventh year (Leviticus 25:4) — the resting member at year-scale.
A counting context never doubles the word: the law says “seven sabbaths,” never seven shabbat shabbaton.

The two senses sort themselves by one rule: numbers count the unit; conduct lands on the day.
Counts take the block — “seven sabbaths shall be complete,” “seven sabbaths of years.”
Conduct takes the day — kindle no fire (Exodus 35:3), bake and seethe beforehand (Exodus 16:23), the offering of the day (Numbers 28:9).
No one heals on a week; no one counts seven of a single day and calls them complete.

Read the commandment again with the unit in view, and notice that it legislates all seven days:

Six days shalt thou labour, and do all thy work: But the seventh day is the sabbath of the LORD thy God…

Both clauses stand inside one commandment — the six of labor are commanded in the same breath as the one of rest.
Scripture lays the six-and-one down seven times.
Creation states it first, before the name exists — six days of making, and on the seventh God shavat, the verb the noun is built on (Genesis 2:2-3); the Law then writes it six times over: the manna (Exodus 16:26), the commandment and its repetition (Exodus 20:9-10; Deuteronomy 5:13-14), the covenant sign (Exodus 31:15), the assembly at Sinai (Exodus 35:2), and the appointed times (Leviticus 23:3) — every one, “six days… but the seventh day is the sabbath.”
Seven times the composition, never once the day alone.
Such repetition is redundant if sabbath names a day defined by rest — a rest-day needs stating once; it is exactly right if the word names a seven defined by the composition of its parts, for a whole is defined by giving all its parts — and Scripture never gives the sabbath any other way.
The same formula runs over the years — “Six years thou shalt sow thy field… but in the seventh year shall be a sabbath of rest unto the land” (Leviticus 25:3-4) — and it outlives Sinai: the ruler of the synagogue recites it against Jesus, “There are six days in which men ought to work… and not on the sabbath day” (Luke 13:14) — a hostile witness, still defining the sabbath by its six.

The sabbath is not an interruption of the week; it is the week made whole, six-and-one as one fabric.
To keep the seventh is to confess the ownership of all seven — the rest-day is one-seventh of what the word names, and the six days of labor are as much inside the sabbath as the rest is.

The block is given, not privately counted.
Israel's first weeks out of Egypt were marked from heaven by the bread itself:

See, for that the LORD hath given you the sabbath, therefore he giveth you on the sixth day the bread of two days; abide ye every man in his place, let no man go out of his place on the seventh day.

Double bread on the sixth day, none on the seventh — a schedule no man could move, marking the whole unit and not merely its end.
The temple ran on the same block: the courses of priests and guards “enter in on the sabbath” and “go forth on the sabbath” (2 Kings 11:5, 7, 9) — a week of duty bounded by the word, service reckoned sabbath to sabbath.

The commandment says “in it thou shalt not do any work” — and the same law commands work in it.

And on the sabbath day two lambs of the first year without spot, and two tenth deals of flour for a meat offering, mingled with oil, and the drink offering thereof: This is the burnt offering of every sabbath, beside the continual burnt offering, and his drink offering.

The offering doubles on the seventh day.
The shewbread is baked and set in order “every sabbath” (Leviticus 24:8; 1 Chronicles 9:32); circumcision proceeds on the sabbath “that the law of Moses should not be broken” (John 7:23).
Jesus states it flatly: “on the sabbath days the priests in the temple profane the sabbath, and are blameless” (Matthew 12:5).
The law that forbids work on the seventh day assigns more of its own work to that day than to any other.

The rest command carries the resolution in its own wording.

If thou turn away thy foot from the sabbath, from doing thy pleasure on my holy day; and call the sabbath a delight, the holy of the LORD, honourable; and shalt honour him, not doing thine own ways, nor finding thine own pleasure, nor speaking thine own words:

The prohibition is possessive — thy pleasure, thine own ways, thine own words — and Hebrews reads the seventh day of creation with the same possessive: “he that is entered into his rest, he also hath ceased from his own works, as God did from his” (Hebrews 4:10).
God's own seventh day was no idle day — “on the seventh day God ended his work” (Genesis 2:2), and the blessing and hallowing of the day are acts of the day; “My Father worketh hitherto, and I work” (John 5:17) is his Son's answer to a sabbath accusation.
The shape of the unit is now complete: six days belong to your work, and the seventh is not empty — it is the day of his: the convocation, the doubled offering, and the mercy that is “lawful to do well on the sabbath days” (Matthew 12:12).
Rest is not the absence of work; it is whose work fills the day.

Now scale the unit by the prophetic day — for “one day is with the Lord as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day” (2 Peter 3:8) — and the sabbath opens into the calendar of the whole age.
Six days of labor, then the day of rest; six thousand years of toil, then “There remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God” (Hebrews 4:9) — and the word there is sabbatismos, a sabbath-keeping.
The thousand-year reign is not an isolated doctrine; it is the seventh-part of a sabbath whose whole is seven thousand years — the great week, complete.
The unit that orders the week and the land and the jubilee orders the age, because it was never a day's name; it was the name of the complete seven at whatever scale the LORD counts.
The great week keeps the six-and-one shape of its smallest copy: “Let us labour therefore to enter into that rest” (Hebrews 4:11) — the labor now, the sabbath ahead.

Scripture reckons time in a standing triad — the feast, the new moon, the sabbath: the year, the month, and the seven between them.
The gate of Ezekiel's vision opens for exactly two kinds of day: the day of the sabbath and the day of the new moon (Ezekiel 46:1-3).
The Shunammite's husband asks why she rides to the prophet when “it is neither new moon, nor sabbath” (2 Kings 4:23); the grain merchants wait out both — “When will the new moon be gone, that we may sell corn? and the sabbath, that we may set forth wheat?” (Amos 8:5); Isaiah's restoration runs “from one new moon to another, and from one sabbath to another” (Isaiah 66:23); Paul lists “an holyday, or of the new moon, or of the sabbath days” as one triad (Colossians 2:16).
The month is divided into sabbaths, and the sabbath into days — and the law itself pins rest-days to the month's dates: at Tabernacles, “on the first day shall be a sabbath, and on the eighth day shall be a sabbath” (Leviticus 23:39) — the fifteenth and the twenty-second of the month.

The count exposes a paradox — and its solution must meet the text exactly.
The omer count is specified three ways at once.
It has a fixed start: the sheaf is waved “on the morrow after the sabbath” (Leviticus 23:11), and the witnesses of the temple age — the Septuagint's rendering, Josephus's report of the practice, Israel's first Passover in the land (Joshua 5:11) — set that sheaf on the sixteenth day of the first month, every year.
It has a unit-count: “seven sabbaths shall be complete.”
And it has a landing condition: “unto the morrow after the seventh sabbath shall ye number fifty days” — the fiftieth day must itself be the morrow after a sabbath.

Try to satisfy all three on an unbroken seven-day cycle, and the system jams.
A fixed sixteenth falls on a different weekday each year; count from it, and the fiftieth day is “the morrow after the sabbath” only one year in seven.
The ancient parties each sawed off one leg to level the stool: some kept the fixed sheaf and let Pentecost land mid-week, abandoning the landing condition; some kept the landing and floated the sheaf to the nearest first-day, abandoning the witnessed sixteenth; some fixed both ends by fiat and abandoned the count between them.
Every camp preserved two specifications by breaking the third — and the breaks are visible, which is the point.

Notice what the continuous week does to the law's own grammar.
On an unbroken cycle, a count of sevens that begins the morrow after a sabbath cannot produce an incomplete seven — the qualifier “complete” would legislate nothing, a dead word in a law where every word has work to do.
Temimot has force only in a reckoning where a broken seven is possible — where the count can meet days that belong to no week.

There is one reckoning in which nothing breaks.
If the month itself is built of four sevens — the sabbaths standing on its eighth, fifteenth, twenty-second, and twenty-ninth days, with the renewed-moon day standing outside the sevens as the month's head — then the fifteenth is a sabbath in every month, the sheaf's sixteenth is always the morrow after the sabbath — and the numbering begins the day after the sheaf.

What remains of the sheaf's own week is six days: a broken seven, exactly what the qualifier “complete” excludes.
So the count gathers seven whole sabbaths — the twenty-third of the first month through the fifteenth of the third, forty-nine days, no broken week and no renewed-moon day among them — and their morrow is the fiftieth: Pentecost on the sixteenth of the third month, the morrow after a sabbath, every year, the very date the Essene witnesses preserve, with no tension left in the text.
Fixed dates and weekday-landings, irreconcilable on the continuous week, agree without effort — and the triple-specified count shows itself for what it is: a checksum, written into the law the way redundancy is written into all Scripture, so that the true calendar passes silently, and every altered one is convicted by its own arithmetic. [Footnote: The full case — the month of four sevens, the renewed-moon days, the witnesses for the fixed sixteenth, and the history of who changed what — is Time Tested Tradition: The Renewed Biblical Calendar; this chapter shows only the lock the key must fit.]

The calendar that keeps these sevens — who kept it, whose testimony carries it, and what tradition did to it — is the next chapter.
